extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, novelists, and literary critics (creative-writing students and teachers)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional lecture-style guidance for analysing and composing novels, focused on two particular aspects: the prophetic/‘song’ quality in fiction and the notion of pattern (and its relation to rhythm) in novel-writing. Uses examples (Dostoevsky, Melville, Lawrence, Brontë, James, Anatole France, Percy Lubbock) to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophet's focus: voice over message
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophetic novelist is not primarily concerned with the prophet's explicit message; what matters is the accent of his voice — his song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by contrast: Hetty's realistic, logically connected dream vs Mitya's prophetic utterance; the critic should value tone, cadence and musicality of expression more than didactic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and suspension of humour required for prophetic fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction 'demands humility and the absence of the sense of humour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reader/critic must be prepared to put aside sniggering or ironic detachment; prophecy asks for a different set of tools and a readiness to accept the work's seriousness even when it offends taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy reaches back (depth) rather than forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic writing 'reaches back' — it seeks depth and an extension of feeling beyond immediate circumstances (though not always to pity and love).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume this means sentimental pity; the reach-back can be aesthetic or metaphysical rather than moral. Examples: Dostoevsky, Melville, Lawrence, Brontë.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spasmodic / intermittent realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction is 'spasmodically realistic' — it can be patiently accurate about commonplace details while simultaneously producing prophetic song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may describe trials, staircases, or catalogues with exactness (Dostoevsky, Melville) and then leap into song; the juxtaposition of meticulous reality and visionary passages is a positive technique, not a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice as song / sound as primary medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction 'gives us the sensation of a song or of sound' — its primary effect is musical or vocal rather than discursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should attend to cadence, repetitions, resonances and the way passages read aloud; examples include the pervasive 'song' in Moby Dick and the storm-sound atmosphere of Wuthering Heights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity-facing orientation (vs fantasy's scattering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike fantasy, prophecy's 'face is towards unity' — its confusion is incidental rather than fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where fantasy playfully digresses or keeps changing mythologies, prophetic fiction aims at a central, unifying pulse that holds the work together; judge works by whether their confusions serve a unifying song rather than accidental disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophet composes from a remoter emotional state and does not reflect
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophet is 'in a remoter emotional state while he composes' and 'does not reflect' or 'hammer away' — composition is more singing than analytic talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid valuing explicit philosophical reflection or workmanlike argument in a prophet's text; Joyce is excluded because he 'undermines the universe in too workmanlike a manner' — talk/analysis undermines song.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roughness of surface as a positive quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic novels often show 'roughness of surface' — dents, grooves, lumps and spikes during reading that provoke immediate reactions but later smooth into unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat apparent textual unevenness, interruptions, or jaggedness as part of the prophetic effect rather than as sloppy workmanship; the roughness can be what makes the work provocative and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic illumination of the mundane
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophet 'manipulates a beam of light' that occasionally illuminates ordinary objects, rendering them more vivid than in domestic realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize passages where ordinary items are suddenly transfigured (Melville's cataloguing of whale-products, Lawrence's evocations of moon-and-water imagery) as evidence of prophetic craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist reductive symbolic reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not convert evocative objects/episodes into simplistic symbols (e.g., 'the Delight' or 'the coffin') because 'even if the symbolism is correct, it silences the book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should preserve the book's song and mystery; over-systematising or imposing a single symbolic gloss can deaden the work's prophetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning often lies outside words; contest + song structure
rubrics_metrics.description: In prophetic works (e.g., Moby Dick) the essential element 'flows athwart the action' and 'lies outside words' — the book is fundamentally a contest whose remainder is song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should allow for non-verbal, affective, and tonal meanings; a summary moral or tidy plot-symbol mapping will often miss the work's core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of evil should transcend petty villainy
rubrics_metrics.description: Real evil in prophetic fiction is not mere sordidness or small vice; it can be personified, grand, proud and non-mercenary (Claggart in Billy Budd is an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge portrayals of depravity by their scale and moral seriousness: prophetic evil may be grave, elevated, and devoid of petty motives — this can be artistically superior to conventional 'villainy' used merely to advance plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophet may preach and agitate; reader must tolerate the bullying tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A prophetic novelist (e.g., D. H. Lawrence) can also be a preacher: his voice may bully, nag, or give hot denunciations and advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and readers should not confuse preaching with lack of artistry; the 'bullying' foreground may coexist with a deeper aesthetic voice — resentment or mockery can make the prophetic treasure disappear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions externalized and atmosphere-driven narration
rubrics_metrics.description: In some prophetic novels (e.g., Wuthering Heights) emotions surround characters like thunder-clouds and generate action; atmosphere and sound can be more important than words or plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate such novels by their ability to externalize passion into landscape, sound and sustained atmosphere rather than by conventional character interiority or plot logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern as an aesthetic aspect drawn mainly from plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern is an aesthetic property of the novel (borrowed from painting) that causes us to see the book as a whole; it 'springs mainly out of the plot' and externalizes beauty as the shape of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify structural shapes (hour-glass, grand chain) and judge how well the plotted events and characters realize an overall pictorial/architectural design (Thais, The Ambassadors, Roman Pictures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern provides pleasure without obvious cause; use pictorial metaphors diagnostically
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern can cause a pleasure 'without knowing why' and pictorial images (hour-glass, grand chain) are helpful explanatory tools but must not be taken literally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors to clarify how the parts form a satisfying whole, but avoid forcing literal geometric readings; the metaphor is diagnostic of aesthetic effect, not a mechanical diagram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern must suit the author's mood and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: A good pattern is appropriate to the author's mood; the same formal shape can be good or bad depending on its fit (Roman Pictures' grand chain suits its sub-acid comic atmosphere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge fit: does the chosen pattern enhance the mood and themes, or does it feel imposed? Assess congruence between structural form and tonal material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern vs rhythm distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: When beauty is the visible 'shape of the book' it is called pattern; when the aesthetic quality is not the book's overall shape but a different kind of musical recurrence, call it rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a novel's unifying beauty is architectural (pattern) or temporal/sonic (rhythm) and apply different critical language accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern can demand artistic sacrifices (limits on character and life)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make pattern 'triumphant' an author may sacrifice scope: few characters, stingily constructed persons, limited sensations, absence of rapid motion or carnality — as in Henry James.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing formally unified novels, note the trade-offs: aesthetic triumph may come at the cost of richness or social realism. Decide whether the sacrifice is justified by the achieved pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader qualities for appreciating pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciation of pattern requires the reader to bring an aesthetic sense able to perceive the book as a whole (to see the 'figure of the Muse' upon neat carpentry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage readers to look beyond plot curiosity and to cultivate sensitivity to how plot, character and atmosphere weave into a larger formal beauty; some readers will not grant the premise required and therefore may not respond.
